10 Four forces, all in the same plane, act on an object.
12 N
20 N
20 N
12 N
What could describe the motion of the object?
A
It is accelerating.
B
It is moving in a straight line.
C
It is moving with decreasing speed.
D
It is moving with increasing momentum.

hints: Notice the diagram pairs: $20\text{ N}$ left against $20\text{ N}$ right, and $12\text{ N}$ up against $12\text{ N}$ down.
Connect those balanced pairs to the vector sum of force and to Newton's first law for zero resultant force.
Compare zero resultant force with what each motion needs: change of velocity or momentum needs net force, while uniform straight-line motion does not.
walkthrough: Look at the diagram: horizontal forces are $20\text{ N}$ to the left and $20\text{ N}$ to the right, vertical forces are $12\text{ N}$ up and $12\text{ N}$ down.
Add components: $20 - 20 = 0$ horizontally and $12 - 12 = 0$ vertically, so the resultant force $F_{net} = 0$.
Use Newton's first law: with $F_{net} = 0$ there is no acceleration, so velocity cannot change in magnitude or direction.
That means the object is either at rest or already moving with constant velocity, which is motion in a straight line at constant speed.
Options A, C and D all require a change in velocity or in momentum $p = mv$, so they need a non-zero resultant force and are ruled out.
Continued uniform straight-line motion is allowed with zero resultant force. This is option B.

A.explanation: Acceleration needs a non-zero resultant force with $F = ma$, but the opposite $20\text{ N}$ and opposite $12\text{ N}$ forces cancel.

B.explanation: Resultant force is zero, so the object can continue in uniform motion in a straight line by Newton's first law.

C.explanation: Decreasing speed needs a resultant force opposite to velocity, but the vector sum of the four forces is zero.

D.explanation: Increasing momentum needs a resultant force from $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$, but the balanced $12\text{ N}$ and $20\text{ N}$ pairs give no change in momentum.
